power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = .930", Sentence = "Interestingly, they found that the regression coefficient for Investigative interests was not statistically significant (b = 0.01; p = .930) in a model without the EVT constructs, but it was statistically significantly negative (b = -0.24; p = .014) when they controlled for the EVT constructs."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Many empirical studies in the social sciences use regression analyses to compare nested models with an increasing number of predictors.
Typically, the focus is on investigating how regression coefficients change when additional predictors are added to a given model.

For instance, a researcher might be interested in the impact of parental socioeconomic status on children's college graduation and how it changes if student achievement is added as a predictor (see the example in Breen et al., 2013).

text.text: The interpretation of such differences in regression coefficients is straightforward for comparisons of samesample nested linear models with continuous outcome variables.
However, the interpretation is generally more complicated for nonlinear models, such as logistic or probit regressions, for two reasons (Karlson et al., 2012).
text.formatted: However, the interpretation is generally more complicated for nonlinear models, such as logistic or probit regressions, for two reasons <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Karlson et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: First, the variance of the assumed underlying latent variable for the categorical outcome is typically not constant across same-sample nested models with different predictors.

Second, the shape of the residual distribution usually changes across models. Karlson et al. (2012) suggested a method, often referred to as the KHB method, in which both the variance of the underlying latent variable of the outcome and the shape of the residual distribution are held constant across nested models.

(2012)</ref> suggested a method, often referred to as the KHB method, in which both the variance of the underlying latent variable of the outcome and the shape of the residual distribution are held constant across nested models.

text.text: The core idea is to hold the predicted part of the underlying latent variable (linear predictor) constant across the models that are being compared.

In the revised KHB method, Breen et al. (2021) presented a modified approach that estimates the full model in a first step and generates the linear predictor, which is subsequently predicted by models with fewer predictors.

text.text: However, in its common implementations (Kohler & Karlson, 2024; Kohler et al., 2011), the KHB method is limited to manifest predictor variables and data sets without missing observations.

text.text: It also cannot easily incorporate nested data structures or survey weights.
In the present paper, we introduce the single-step pseudo mediation model (PMM) and show how this model implements the multistep KHB method within a structural equation modeling (SEM) framework.
We demonstrate how differences between and ratios of regression coefficients from a sequence of same-sample nested models can be estimated using coefficients from a single full model.

This specification solves typical challenges in the analysis of empirical data, such as (a) missing values, (b) measurement error in the predictors, and (c) complex data structures with clustering and survey weights.

In current implementations of the (revised) KHB method, either all observations with any missing values on the variables of interest have to be excluded from the analysis (listwise deletion, see, e.g., Xie & He, 2025) or the data have to be (multiply) imputed before the analysis (see, e.g., Domènech-Abella et al., 2018).

text.text: This generated linear predictor variable 𝑉𝑉 is then used as an outcome variable in a series of linear (OLS) regression models that estimate the regression coefficients with a stepwise inclusion of predictors.
Suppose there is a full model with two predictors 𝑥𝑥 1 and 𝑥𝑥 2 .
In a first step, the regression coefficients for both predictors are estimated, for instance, in a logistic regression model.
Based on the resulting estimates of both regression coefficients, the linear predictor is generated as 𝑉𝑉 = β 1 𝑥𝑥 1 + β 2 𝑥𝑥 2 .
The regression coefficient for a model including only 𝑥𝑥 1 is then estimated in a second step by regressing 𝑉𝑉 on 𝑥𝑥 1 in a linear regression.

This approach is analogous to the classical mediation approach in linear models where the total effect for 𝑥𝑥 1 is estimated in a model including only 𝑥𝑥 1 as a predictor, and the indirect effect is estimated as the difference between this total effect and the effect of 𝑥𝑥 1 on the outcome in a second model that also includes 𝑥𝑥 2 (MacKinnon, 2008).

text.text: Although conceptually related, the revised KHB approach is different from the single-step PMM approach, as the revised KHB approach still relies on a series of models to be estimated, whereas all coefficients for different target models are obtained from a single model in the PMM approach.
The PMM approach takes advantage of the flexibility of SEM implementations to easily and appropriately handle challenges commonly encountered in the analysis of realistically complex empirical data.

text.text: We demonstrate the equivalence of our PMM approach with the revised KHB method in a simulation study with three predictors that were either uncorrelated or correlated.

Comparing coefficients from same-sample nested models is not as straightforward in linear probability models (e.g., logistic or probit regression) as in linear regression because the regression coefficients in nested models might change even if a predictor is included in a model that is uncorrelated with all the other predictors.
To handle this problem, Karlson et al. (2012) suggested a method in which the distribution of the underlying latent variable of the outcome is held constant across nested models (the KHB method).

text.text: In the present paper, we introduced the PMM and embedded it in an SEM framework.

Then we showed in our simulation study and in one of our empirical examples that the PMM produces results that are equivalent to the (revised) KHB method under the same assumptions (observed data from a simple random sample without missing values).
The PMM can easily be implemented in Mplus via the code templates or our SAS macro, which generates the necessary Mplus code.

Compared with the (revised) KHB method, we demonstrated in our empirical examples, which were based on Wille et al. (2020), that the PMM has at least three advantages (if implemented in Mplus): First, missing values can be adequately handled under MAR assumptions with FIML instead of listwise deletion or multiple imputation.

(2020)</ref>, that the PMM has at least three advantages (if implemented in Mplus): First, missing values can be adequately handled under MAR assumptions with FIML instead of listwise deletion or multiple imputation.

text.text: Second, complex sampling designs (e.g., cluster sampling, survey weights) can be taken into account, for instance, by applying a cluster bootstrap with or without survey weights.

Third, latent variables can be included as predictors or covariates that-assuming an adequate specification of the measurement model-may be preferable to point estimates (e.g., factor scores) that contain measurement error and may lead to biased results.
For inferential statistics, the results from a bootstrapping procedure (e.g., the lower and upper limits of a CI) always depend on randomly drawn bootstrap samples.

In simulation studies with a rather large number of Monte Carlo samples, even relatively small numbers of bootstrap samples lead to valid results with regard to the coverage of confidence intervals (Gaigall & Gerstenberg, 2026).

text.text: In a specific statistical application, however, a larger number of bootstrap samples may be recommended for two reasons (Hesterberg, 2011): First, results are more likely to converge across different software implementations.
text.formatted: In a specific statistical application, however, a larger number of bootstrap samples may be recommended for two reasons <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Hesterberg, 2011)</ref>: First, results are more likely to converge across different software implementations.

text.text: Second, compared with the cost of the data in terms of money, time, and so forth, the cost of the analysis is typically of minor importance.

Thus, the gain in the precision of a CI (e.g., due to a larger number of bootstrap samples) is less expensive than increasing the sample size. Hesterberg (2011), for instance, suggested 15,000 bootstrap samples for a bootstrap percentile interval "to have 95% probability that the actual one-sided noncoverage for a 95% bootstrap interval falls within 10% of the desired value, between 0.0225 and 0.0275" (p. 522).
text.formatted: Thus, the gain in the precision of a CI (e.g., due to a larger number of bootstrap samples) is less expensive than increasing the sample size. <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Hesterberg (2011)</ref>, for instance, suggested 15,000 bootstrap samples for a bootstrap percentile interval "to have 95% probability that the actual one-sided noncoverage for a 95% bootstrap interval falls within 10% of the desired value, between 0.0225 and 0.0275" (p. 522).

text.text: Therefore, for applied researchers, approximately 15,000 bootstrap samples would be advisable for 95% CIs, provided that number of samples is computationally feasible in terms of memory capacity and computation time.

Otherwise, it may be difficult for other researchers to closely replicate a given CI when using different software, as the lower and upper limits of the CI are less accurate approximations of the respective percentiles of the theoretical bootstrap distribution.
The PMM can be applied to a large variety of different contexts, including scenarios with missing data, complex sampling, and latent variable models.
With the bootstrap approach, reliable standard errors and accurate nonsymmetric CIs for the estimated coefficients can be expected in many different scenarios.

Bootstrapping, however, might not be feasible for (very) complex (latent variable) models because of the high computational demand, and standard error estimation for (grand) indirect effects based on (robust) maximum likelihood estimation might be preferred in such cases.
However, symmetric confidence intervals calculated with this method may fail to achieve the intended 1-α coverage probability.
In simulation studies, the first-order or Sobel test (Sobel, 1982) for indirect effects, for instance, showed low power rates and low Type I error rates (MacKinnon et al., 2002).
text.formatted: In simulation studies, the first-order or Sobel test <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Sobel, 1982)</ref> for indirect effects, for instance, showed low power rates and low Type I error rates <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(MacKinnon et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: In such cases, Bayesian estimation of the PMM might be a viable alternative to maximum likelihood approaches.

Regarding ordered-categorical outcomes with more than two categories, even though we did not discuss such cases in the present study, the PMM can easily be applied (e.g., in Mplus where such outcomes can be handled as well).
In such cases, the outcome is represented by a single latent response variable 𝑦𝑦 * , and all equations that include the regression coefficients for the predictors and covariates are valid.
For the thresholds, however, the respective equations must be applied to each threshold in cases with more than two outcome categories.
Furthermore, researchers can use our SAS macro %revKHB to estimate coefficients for ordered-categorical outcomes via the bootstrap-based revised KHB method.
In applied research, the specific research questions about categorical outcomes are often addressed by applying logistic or probit regression models.
Compared with other approaches, the statistical hypotheses that can be addressed with the KHB method may often be seen as the most adequate for such research questions.

We propose that researchers integrate the KHB method's strength in ensuring regression coefficient comparability across models with the capacity of SEM to handle missing data via FIML, accommodate survey weights, and incorporate latent variables.
The suggested PMM framework is a simple way of combining the best of both worlds.
